Traditionally, a database is organized as a collection of files, which are updated in place. However, if the database crashes after an update has been written to some of the files but not to others, the update is lost. A write-ahead log allows the database to recover the lost update by considering the sequence of updates stored in the log before the crash.
When a database adapts the write-ahead log, it stores each update in the log before applying the update to the database files. If the database crashes and the log has been partially written, the database can replay the updates stored in the log to bring the data files up to the point of the crash. In other words, the log can be used as a backup of the last bit of data that was written to the files. By replaying the unsecured updates from the log, the database can recover the correct state of the data files and continue processing where it left off.
The write-ahead log also allows the database to recover from a crash because it provides a total ordering of all updates. In other words, the log ensures that each update is associated with a specific sequence number that determines the order in which the updates should be applied.
